newsitem.title: JAPAN: Deutsche Telekom pins high hopes on Tokyo bourse.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom pins high hopes on Tokyo bourse.

text.p: Confident Deutsche Telekom AG officials said on Friday the German firm's forthcoming share listing could be the biggest by a foreign company in the Asia-Pacific region if demand lives up to expectations.
Company officials expect that up to eight percent of the 500 million shares they will offer worldwide this month will be scooped up in the region.

"The five to eight percent indicative tranche size for the Asia-Pacific region could mean that Deutsche Telekom was the largest offering in the region to date," said Joachim Kroeske, the company's chief finance officer.
"This underlines the importance of the Asia-Pacific region to us," he said.

Germany's telecommunications monopoly is due to list about 500 million of its shares globally, starting with the Frankfurt and New York bourses on November 18, followed by the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) a day later.
After the first tranche, Telekom will be worth up to an estimated 75 billion marks ($49.34 billion) based on an expected price range of between 25 marks ($16.45) and 30 marks ($19.74) per share.
Telekom executives were on the Japan leg of a roadshow to woo investors. They were joined by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who visited the TSE to help with the promotion.
The state-owned firm's listing on the TSE's foreign stock section will be the first by a U.S. or European firm since 1993.
Nearly five years ago the exchange boasted 127 foreign issues, but low liquidity, enormous costs and a strong yen against the dollar brought on an exodus.
This year 11 firms have delisted so far, and after Exxon Corp leaves in December, only 66 firms will be left, TSE officials said.
Telekom said it was keen to list here, as Japan is the second-largest capital market in the world after New York.
"We want to widen our range of investors, not only in the retail side but also on the institutional side," Kroeske said.
However, Japanese market sources were sceptical about the success of the shares in Japan.

"Liquidity is non-existent in the foreign section," a second-tier brokerage broker said. "When the shares are listed, it will attract some attention and there may be some trading done, but it will soon fizzle out."
Some brokers said the nature of the shares could also be a discouraging factor for investors planning to trade the shares to obtain profits.
"Investors buy German stocks to take advantage of high dividend yields," said Kenzo Doi, a Kokusai Securities strategist.

Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities, said the shares were not likely to be heavily traded in the long run, but added the listing could spice up trade in Japanese telecommunications shares.
"Japan's telecommunications industry is heading for deregulation and is seen becoming the focus of trade," Ueki said. "Telekom is a solid, stable company and its listing will encourage investors."
Telekom chief executive officer Ron Sommer said the firm was looking into the possibility of a tie-up with Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, but he did not elaborate.

Officials said if the shares listed on the TSE are snapped up, the telecommunications giant may consider going public on other Asian exchanges such as Hong Kong and Singapore a year after the Tokyo listing. ($1=1.52 marks)
